newsitem.title: UK: UK union chiefs say workers want more under Labour.
newsitem.headline: UK union chiefs say workers want more under Labour.

text.p: British trade union leaders said on Sunday that workers had high hopes of the newly elected Labour government, which may not realistically be able to meet all their expectations.

John Monks, General Secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the unions' umbrella body, said he felt workers in Britain deserved better treatment than they had experienced under the Conservative government defeated on May 1.
"I think the case will be made, and certainly be made by the TUC, for better protection for people at work," Monks told BBC-2 television's The Money Programme.

"One of the curses of Britain over the last period has been rising inequality -- some people at the top getting ridiculous amounts of money -- and rising job insecurity with the casualisation of so much work.
"We will be campaigning for better checks against those kinds of abuses," Monks said.
New Prime Minister Tony Blair, who has has abandoned many of the Labour Party's socialist principles, has also scrapped some of its traditional promises to the unions.
In particular, he has discarded a commitment to extend legal protections and minimum rights to all workers from their first day in a job -- a source of friction with the unions.

Tony Young, General Secretary of the Communications Workers' Union, said that after 18 years of an anti-trade union government, there may be some people in the CWU who will want more than the new government can realistically deliver.

"I don't think I like the word payback because I think that describes the wrong kind of relationship but I think there are some clear commitments that the party has made on a range of issues that we see as fundamentally important.
"We've had 18 years of pent-up frustration, if you like, and there will be I'm sure those in the movement who will want to see a lot more delivered than perhaps is possible," Young said.
Lew Adams, General Secretary of the rail union ASLEF, said he felt positive about the scope for trade unions under the new Labour government.
"I've got a feeling that Tony Blair might be more radical than people might think," he said.
He said he accepted that the railway industry could not be renationalised overnight, but added:
"I think the Labour government will accept there's going to be some form of timetable and we shall look again at the railway industry and see what we can do," Adams said.
